name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
one_sentence_pitch: Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS). 2.
plain_summary: Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS). 2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. 3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. 4.
objectives: Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS). 2.
Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. 3.
Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. 4.
Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. 5.
method: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.
main_findings: Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation.
The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses.
These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion.
However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames.
safety_relevance: Supports NASA’s prevention and detection pillars of spacecraft fire safety.
